challenges.text: A school orders 6 kits. Each kit has x pencils and 4 markers. Write the total number of tools two ways. For x = 7, find the total. Explain why 6x + 4 is incorrect.

challenges.text: Two rectangular banners are both 3 m high. Their widths are x m and x + 2 m. Write their combined area in a simplified form. Find it for x = 4. Can one rectangle show the same area?

discussion.expect: 6x + 6 square m; 30 square m; one 3 m by (2x + 2) m rectangle.

deepening.title: One rectangle, three expressions
deepening.prompt: A rectangle has height 4 and width 2x+3. Ari writes 4(2x+3), Bo writes 8x+12, and Cy writes 8x+3. Decide which expressions match for every x. Use a split rectangle, then test x=2. Explain why testing one value can disprove a claim but cannot establish every-value equivalence.
deepening.answer: Ari and Bo are equivalent; Cy is not. At x=2 the values are 28, 28, 19.
deepening.worked: Split the width into 2x and 3. The pieces have areas 8x and 12, so 4(2x+3)=8x+12 for all allowed lengths. Cy counts only 3 square units in the second piece instead of 12. A mismatch disproves equivalence; a structural argument proves it.
deepening.teacher_ask: Which part of the rectangle accounts for the constant 12?
deepening.teacher_hint: Trace the height 4 on both parts; do not add the labels as lengths from different directions.
deepening.visual_hint: Rectangle height 4 split into widths 2x and 3; label piece areas only during the reveal.
steps: Split the width into 2x and 3; both parts have height 4.
At x=2, Ari and Bo both give 28; Cy gives 19. A structural split explains every-value equivalence.

discussion_moves: Ask the learner to explain why both terms are multiplied.
Compare a numerical check with a diagram that works for any positive x.
Invite a different split, such as x+x+3, and combine its areas.

deepening.title: A solution and a changing relationship
deepening.prompt: A pool contains 6 liters and gains 3 liters each minute. Compare the equation 6+3t=24 with the rule L=6+3t. Solve the equation, build rule outputs for t=0, 2, 6, and explain why the rule has many pairs but the equation asks for one time.
deepening.worked: The equation fixes the final amount at 24. Subtract 6 then divide by 3 to get 6 minutes. The rule accepts each time and returns a different water amount; its graph starts above the origin at 6 liters.
deepening.teacher_ask: Which quantity is fixed in the equation and which may vary in the rule?
deepening.teacher_hint: Cover L with 24 to turn the rule into the one-question equation.
deepening.visual_hint: Table and first-quadrant graph of L=6+3t; highlight (6, 24).
steps: At zero minutes the pool already has 6 liters.
The rule L=6+3t gives 6, 12, 24 liters at 0, 2, 6 minutes.
Set L=24: remove 6, then divide 18 by 3 to get 6 minutes.

discussion_moves: Ask what zero minutes means in this context.
Have the student check the solved time in the original equation.
Compare the water added with the total water present.
